title: Mental Health Concepts and History of Psychiatric Care
body:
## What it is
Mental health is a state of emotional, psychological and social wellness shown by satisfying relationships, effective behavior and coping, a positive self-concept and emotional stability. A mental disorder is a clinically significant behavioral or psychological pattern that comes with distress or disability, or with a raised risk of suffering, pain, death or loss of freedom.

## Must-know facts
- Components of mental health: autonomy and independence, reaching one's potential, tolerating life's uncertainties, self-esteem, mastery of the environment, reality orientation and stress management.
- Ancient times: illness was seen as the gods' displeasure. People with mental illness were thought divine (worshipped) or demonic (punished or burned). Aristotle's humoral idea tied mood to balance of body fluids; treatment was bloodletting, starving and purging.
- Early Christian era: illness blamed on demons and possession; treatment was exorcism, then dungeons, flogging and starvation if it failed.
- Renaissance: the mentally ill began to be separated from criminals. Harmless people wandered; dangerous ones were jailed and chained. The Hospital of St. Mary of Bethlehem was the first hospital for the insane, but inmates were treated like animals. Witch hunts also happened.
- Enlightenment: Philippe Pinel and William Tuke created the idea of the asylum as a safe refuge. Dorothea Dix pushed for adequate shelter, food and warm clothing.
- Emil Kraepelin classified mental disorders by symptoms; Eugene Bleuler coined the term schizophrenia.

## Why the trend matters
The story moves from blame and punishment to shelter, then to classification and humane treatment. Exam items usually ask who is credited with what.

## How the exam asks about it
Match a name to a contribution (Pinel and Tuke: asylum; Dix: humane conditions; Kraepelin: classification; Bleuler: schizophrenia). Another common item asks for a sign of good mental health.

## Memory aid
Invented: Pinel and Tuke give a "place of safety"; Dix gives the "daily needs"; Kraepelin "categorizes"; Bleuler "names schizophrenia".

## Related topics
[[Psychiatric Nursing Overview]], [[Therapeutic Use of Self and Johari's Window]], [[Nurse-Patient Relationship Phases]]

## Check against your textbook
- The handout gave the Aristotle humor idea; many books credit Hippocrates. Check who your textbook names.
outlineRefs: Historical Perspectives of the Treatment of Mental Illness

title: Therapeutic Use of Self and Johari's Window
body:
## What it is
Therapeutic use of self means the nurse uses his or her own personality and presence as the main tool for building a helping relationship. Hildegard Peplau (1952) stressed that a nurse who understands herself can help the client grow.

## Must-know facts
- It depends on self-awareness: knowing your own feelings, beliefs and attitudes.
- Goal of self-awareness: keep your values and biases from being projected onto the client and interfering with care.
- Johari's Window has four quadrants:
  - Quadrant I, open (arena or public self): known to you and to others.
  - Quadrant II, blind self: known to others but not to you.
  - Quadrant III, hidden (facade or private self): known only to you.
  - Quadrant IV, unknown: not yet discovered by you or anyone.
- Ways to grow self-awareness: role play, introspection, discussion with others (feedback), and enlarging your experience.
- In the pre-orientation phase the main task is developing self-awareness; see [[Nurse-Patient Relationship Phases]].

## Priority nursing actions
1. Reflect on your own reaction before reacting to a difficult client.
2. Ask for feedback to shrink the blind quadrant.
3. Notice countertransference and discuss it in supervision.

## How the exam asks about it
Identify the quadrant from a description (a trait that coworkers see but the nurse does not is the blind self), or name the nurse's main tool.

## Related topics
[[Therapeutic Communication]], [[Mental Health Concepts and History of Psychiatric Care]]

## Check against your textbook
- The handout credits Peplau for the term; confirm in your own text.

title: Group, Milieu and Family Therapy
body:
## What it is
These are therapies that use the people and surroundings around the client. Each treats the client in a social setting rather than one-to-one.

## Must-know facts
- Group therapy: three or more clients with a therapist to relieve emotional difficulty, build self-esteem, gain insight and improve relationships. Minimum three members; ideal group is 8 to 10.
- Types of group:
  - Therapeutic group: insight into problems (Alcoholics Anonymous is the handout's example).
  - Socialization group: improves interaction among clients.
  - Life review or reminiscing group: lessens isolation, often for older adults.
- Milieu therapy: planned control of the environment so that the setting itself promotes positive change. The nurse looks at what each client needs while remembering the needs of the whole group.
- Family therapy: treats the family as an interacting system; the handout lists it as best suited when there is domestic violence.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Keep the unit safe, predictable and structured (milieu).
2. In a group, set rules, keep confidentiality, and make sure everyone has a chance to take part.
3. In family work, involve all members and avoid taking sides.

## How the exam asks about it
Choose the therapy that matches the goal (isolation in older adults: reminiscing group; changing the unit environment: milieu) or state group size.

## Related topics
[[Behavioral Management, Restraints and De-escalation]], [[Alcohol Use Disorder]], [[Expressive and Insight Therapies]]

## Check against your textbook
- Many books describe family therapy as useful for many family problems, not only domestic violence; check your text.

title: Expressive and Insight Therapies
body:
## What it is
A set of talk, art, play and relaxation approaches used on the psychiatric unit, from deep exploration of the unconscious to simple activities that ease tension.

## Must-know facts
- Psychoanalysis: explores the unconscious and the client's defenses. Behavior problems are linked to unresolved, anxiety-provoking childhood experiences that were repressed. Goal: bring them into awareness and learn healthier coping. Tools: dream analysis and free association (saying thoughts aloud without censoring).
- Hypnotherapy: induces a trance in which the client is highly open to instruction.
- Remotivation therapy: discussion of neutral topics to promote expression of feelings. Reality orientation suits rehabilitation clients, not clients who are actively psychotic.
- Music therapy: relaxation, expression of feelings and release of tension.
- Play therapy: lets a child feel intense emotion safely through play; dolls are used with abused children.
- Humor therapy: laughter eases tension that comes with serious matters and encourages interaction.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Match the therapy to the client's level of function and safety.
2. Do not push reality orientation on a client who is acutely psychotic; that may increase agitation.
3. Observe and record the client's responses.

## How the exam asks about it
Pick the therapy for a described goal (child abuse victim: play therapy with dolls; free association: psychoanalysis).

## Related topics
[[Freud's Theory and Defense Mechanisms]], [[Group, Milieu and Family Therapy]], [[Behavior Modification and Reinforcement]]

title: Behavior Modification and Reinforcement
body:
## What it is
Behavior modification applies learning principles to change maladaptive behavior. It strengthens a wanted behavior by reinforcement.

## Must-know facts
- Positive reinforcement: giving something pleasant after the behavior, such as attention and praise. Example: a group leader praises the client each time he uses assertive communication.
- Negative reinforcement: removing something unpleasant right after the behavior so the behavior is more likely to be repeated. Example: an anxious client volunteers to speak first so the anxious waiting ends.
- Both increase the behavior. Negative reinforcement is NOT punishment.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Define the target behavior clearly.
2. Reinforce the desired behavior immediately and consistently.
3. Keep all staff using the same plan.

## How the exam asks about it
Differentiate positive from negative reinforcement: ask whether something was added or removed, and whether the behavior increased.

## Related topics
[[Developmental Disorders]], [[Expressive and Insight Therapies]], [[Behavioral Management, Restraints and De-escalation]]

title: Electroconvulsive Therapy
body:
## What it is
Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) delivers a brief electric current to the brain under anesthesia to produce a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. A seizure is the sign it worked.

## Must-know facts
- Used for severe depression that does not respond to drugs, and for clients actively suicidal who cannot wait weeks for an antidepressant. Also listed: mania, catatonia and schizophrenia.
- Typical course: 6 to 12 treatments (up to 15), given with about 48 hours between sessions (commonly three per week). Current lasts about 0.5 to 2 seconds.
- Needs informed consent.
- Medications: atropine to reduce secretions, methohexital as the short-acting anesthetic, succinylcholine as the muscle relaxant to soften the seizure. The brain is monitored with EEG.
- High-risk conditions: raised intracranial pressure, recent fracture, cardiac disease, retinal detachment, pregnancy.
- Complications: memory loss, headache, apnea, respiratory depression, fracture.

## Priority nursing actions
Before:
1. Confirm signed consent, NPO after midnight, have the client void, start an IV, remove dentures and jewelry.
After (airway first, ABCs):
1. Ventilate with 100% oxygen until the client breathes unassisted, and watch breathing.
2. Reorient to time, place and person; expect brief confusion and short-term memory loss.
3. Observe until oriented and steady, especially when first standing; protect from falls.
4. Give a benzodiazepine if ordered for agitation; document the treatment.

## Client and family teaching
- Temporary confusion and memory gaps are common and usually improve; treatments are repeated over weeks.

## How the exam asks about it
Priority after ECT is airway and breathing, then reorientation and safety. Another item asks for a contraindication or the purpose of each drug.

## Related topics
[[Major Depressive Disorder]], [[Bipolar Disorder and Mania]], [[Schizophrenia]]

## Check against your textbook
- The handout lists the voltage as "70-50 volts", which looks garbled; verify. Whether schizophrenia and mania are indications varies by source.

title: Crisis Types, Phases and Intervention Styles
body:
## What it is
Fills out the handout's view of crisis: how crises are grouped, how they progress, and the two ways a nurse can intervene. See [[Crisis and Crisis Intervention]] for the core concept.

## Must-know facts
- Features of a crisis: highly individual, usually lasts about 4 to 6 weeks, the person becomes passive and dependent, and the support system is affected.
- Maturational (developmental): expected and predictable life events, such as leaving home, marriage, having a baby, starting a career.
- Situational (accidental): sudden and unexpected external events, such as death of a loved one, job loss, illness or an accident.
- Social (adventitious): disasters and violence, such as floods, earthquakes, war, terrorism, riots, rape or murder.
- Four phases: denial; increased tension (still doing daily activities); disorganization (cannot do daily activities); attempts to reorganize (previous coping mechanisms mobilized).
- Goal of crisis intervention: reach the best possible level of functioning.
- Authoritative style: assesses, gives information, raises self-awareness through feedback, and directs behavior with suggestions.
- Facilitative style: meets the need for empathy by encouraging the client to name feelings, acting as a sounding board and affirming self-worth.
- The nurse's role is active and directive.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Assess safety first.
2. Take a directive approach during disorganization.
3. Encourage use of past successful coping and support people.

## How the exam asks about it
Classify the crisis from a short story, or identify the phase from what the client can still do.

## Related topics
[[Trauma and Stressor-Related Disorders]], [[Rape, Rape Trauma Syndrome and Survivor Care]], [[Disaster Management Continuum]]

## Check against your textbook
- Other books describe different phase counts and durations; use the model your course teaches.
outlineRefs: Primary Role of the Nurse in Crisis

title: Rape, Rape Trauma Syndrome and Survivor Care
body:
## What it is
Rape is a crime of violence and humiliation expressed through sexual means. It is generally an act of hostility, anger or violence, not of sexual desire. Under Philippine law (RA 8353) the act includes insertion of the penis into the mouth, vagina or anus without consent. Consent is not valid if the victim was forced, threatened, drugged or intoxicated, mentally incapable of judging, or below the age of consent.

## Must-know facts
- Power rape: the aim is to command and master the victim; the rapist feels inadequate and uses rape to prove potency.
- Sadistic rape: brutality, bondage and torture; the assault itself is eroticized.
- Rape trauma syndrome phases: acute (shock, numbness, disbelief); denial (refuses to talk about it); heightened anxiety (fear, tension, nightmares); reorganization (life normalizes).

## Priority nursing actions
1. Give immediate emotional support in a private, safe place; stay with the client.
2. Let her proceed at her own pace; do not rush interviews or examination.
3. Return control: let her decide whom to call and what happens next.
4. Preserve evidence (a priority in care); consent must be signed before photographs and before hair and nail samples are taken. Avoid bathing or changing clothes before collection.
5. Offer prophylaxis for sexually transmitted infection and pregnancy; HIV testing may be encouraged; refer to a rape crisis center.
6. The decision to file charges and testify belongs to the victim.

## How the exam asks about it
Best response: nonjudgmental support and client control. Wrong answers push the victim, blame her, or reassure falsely.

## Related topics
[[Crisis Types, Phases and Intervention Styles]], [[Trauma and Stressor-Related Disorders]], [[VAWC and Violence Against Women and Children]]

## Check against your textbook
- The handout describes rape only for female victims; RA 8353 also covers sexual assault of any person, and male survivors need the same care. Check the law and local protocols (Women and Children Protection Unit).
outlineRefs: Phases of the Rape Trauma Syndrome

title: Extrapyramidal Symptoms and Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome
body:
## What it is
Movement side effects of antipsychotics, caused by dopamine (D2) blockade in the brain's motor pathways, plus the dangerous neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS). See [[Typical and Atypical Antipsychotics]] for the drug classes.

## Must-know facts
- Acute dystonia (early, an emergency): torticollis, opisthotonus, oculogyric crisis, muscle rigidity and cramping, thick tongue, difficulty swallowing, laryngospasm, respiratory difficulty. Treat with IM benztropine or IM or IV diphenhydramine.
- Pseudoparkinsonism: stooped posture, mask-like face, reduced arm swing, shuffling festinating gait, cogwheel rigidity, drooling, pill-rolling at rest. Treat by changing to a drug with fewer EPS, or adding an anticholinergic or amantadine.
- Akathisia: cannot sit still, restless, anxious. Treat by changing the drug or adding a beta-blocker, anticholinergic or benzodiazepine.
- Tardive dyskinesia: worm-like tongue movements, lip smacking, involuntary body movements; appears after prolonged therapy (handout says at least 8 months), may be permanent. Valbenazine and deutetrabenazine are used; lowering the antipsychotic may stop progression.
- NMS: potentially fatal reaction with rigidity, high fever, unstable blood pressure, sweating, pallor, delirium, and swings from agitation to stupor. Stop all antipsychotics at once and treat dehydration and hyperthermia.
- Drugs used for EPS include amantadine, benztropine, biperiden, procyclidine, trihexyphenidyl, diphenhydramine, diazepam and propranolol.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Airway first: laryngospasm or trouble swallowing in dystonia is an emergency.
2. Fever plus rigidity: hold the drug, call the provider, cool and hydrate.
3. Screen regularly for tardive dyskinesia.
4. Teach the client to report stiffness, restlessness or fever.

## How the exam asks about it
Name the EPS from a description, choose the first drug for dystonia, or pick NMS signs over EPS signs (fever and autonomic instability).

## Related topics
[[Schizophrenia]], [[Antidepressants and Mood Stabilizers]], [[Lithium Therapy and Toxicity]]

## Check against your textbook
- Time frame for tardive dyskinesia varies; verify. Dosing is not given here.

title: Lithium Therapy and Toxicity
body:
## What it is
Lithium is the best-established mood stabilizer for bipolar disorder. It steadies mood, prevents highs and lows, and treats acute mania. Other mood stabilizers include carbamazepine, valproic acid, gabapentin and lamotrigine. See [[Antidepressants and Mood Stabilizers]].

## Must-know facts
- Forms: tablets, capsules and sustained-release liquid; no injectable form.
- Handout levels: normal 0.5 to 1.5 mEq/L; therapeutic 0.6 to 1.2 mEq/L. Above 3.0 mEq/L, dialysis is considered.
- Common side effects: mild nausea and diarrhea, loss of appetite, fine hand tremor, increased thirst and urination, metallic taste, fatigue.
- Toxic signs: severe vomiting and diarrhea, muscle weakness, poor coordination; untreated can lead to kidney failure, coma and death.
- Valproic acid: can cause liver failure. Carbamazepine: aplastic anemia and agranulocytosis. Lamotrigine: Stevens-Johnson syndrome (severe rash).

## Priority nursing actions
1. Check serum levels regularly; hold the dose and report toxic signs.
2. Give with food to reduce nausea.
3. Keep sodium and fluid intake normal; avoid heavy sweating and dehydration because lithium levels rise quickly.
4. For tremor, a beta-blocker such as propranolol may be requested.
5. Expect some weight gain; teach a balanced diet and exercise.
6. Anticonvulsants: sedation can be eased with the larger dose at bedtime.

## How the exam asks about it
Recognize toxicity (coarse tremor, vomiting, ataxia), choose the safest advice (steady salt and fluids), or match adverse effects to each mood stabilizer.

## Related topics
[[Bipolar Disorder and Mania]], [[Extrapyramidal Symptoms and Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome]]

## Check against your textbook
- Verify the target level (many books give 0.8 to 1.2 mEq/L) and when to draw the level (about 12 hours after the last dose).

title: Antianxiety Drugs: Benzodiazepines and Buspirone
body:
## What it is
Anxiolytics treat anxiety, insomnia, alcohol withdrawal, and sometimes OCD, depression and post-traumatic stress. Benzodiazepines are the most effective for quick relief.

## Must-know facts
- Benzodiazepines in the handout: alprazolam, chlordiazepoxide, clonazepam, diazepam, flurazepam, lorazepam, oxazepam, temazepam, triazolam. Buspirone is a non-benzodiazepine option (non-sedating, slow onset).
- They relieve symptoms; they do not treat the cause of anxiety.
- They strongly add to the effect of alcohol: one drink may act like three.
- Drowsiness: avoid driving and dangerous tasks.
- Withdrawal from benzodiazepines can be fatal; never stop abruptly without medical supervision.
- Take only as prescribed.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Safety: fall precautions, sedation and respiratory checks.
2. Teach no alcohol, no abrupt stopping, no driving until effect is known.
3. Encourage non-drug coping skills with the medication.

## How the exam asks about it
Pick the teaching point (no alcohol, taper off) or the drug with low abuse risk and slow action (buspirone).

## Related topics
[[Anxiety and Anxiety Disorders]], [[Alcohol Use Disorder]], [[Downers: Barbiturates and Opioids]]

## Check against your textbook
- The handout calls the SSRIs the safest drug for panic attacks; many books place benzodiazepines for fast relief. Verify.

title: Autism Spectrum Disorder
body:
## What it is
A neurodevelopmental disorder with impaired communication and social interaction plus stereotyped behaviors, interests and activities. It is more common in boys, shows before about 3 years of age, has a genetic link, and is treatable but not curable. The main problem is impaired interpersonal functioning.

## Must-know facts
- Signs: little eye contact, few facial expressions or gestures, does not relate to peers and parents, little spontaneous enjoyment, flat affect, little intelligible speech, stereotyped movements (hand flapping, body twisting, head banging), may seem deaf, no fear of danger.
- Tantrums may include head banging.
- Low-dose antipsychotic may be used for severe behaviors.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Safety first: risk for injury is the priority diagnosis. Protect from head banging with a helmet and padded surroundings; observe closely, even 1:1.
2. Keep a consistent routine and introduce change slowly.
3. Use short, simple sentences when speaking.
4. Offer small, frequent, balanced meals for nutrition below body needs.
5. Support the family (love and belonging): family therapy and parent teaching.

## How the exam asks about it
Priority diagnosis is risk for injury; best approach is routine, short sentences and consistent staff.

## Related topics
[[Developmental Disorders]], [[Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder]], [[Intellectual Disability]]

## Check against your textbook
- The handout line "all vowels" under communication is unclear and was left out. Current criteria are usually described as one spectrum, not separate diagnoses.

title: Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder
body:
## What it is
A childhood disorder of inattention, overactivity and impulsiveness, more common in boys, diagnosed around preschool or school entry (symptoms before age 7 in the handout).

## Must-know facts
- Causes: unknown; linked to neurologic impairment, early malnutrition, reduced frontal lobe blood flow, and drugs, alcohol or tobacco in pregnancy.
- Risks: family history, relatives with antisocial personality disorder, lower socioeconomic status, male sex, family discord.
- Inattentive: misses details, careless mistakes, cannot sustain attention, seems not to listen, does not finish chores, disorganized, avoids mental effort, loses things.
- Hyperactive-impulsive: fidgets, leaves seat, runs and climbs, cannot play quietly, always on the go, talks too much, blurts, interrupts, cannot wait turn.
- Stimulants: methylphenidate, dextroamphetamine, pemoline. Side effects: loss of appetite, weight loss, nausea, irritability, dizziness, dry mouth, blurred vision, palpitations. Pemoline can cause life-threatening liver failure.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Safety: stop unsafe behavior, supervise closely, give clear limits.
2. Give methylphenidate after meals to limit appetite loss; give dextroamphetamine's last dose early afternoon to prevent insomnia. Monitor weight and height (growth).
3. Simplify directions: get full attention, break tasks into small steps, allow breaks.
4. Keep a structured daily routine with few changes; quiet place for tasks.
5. Offer finger foods; avoid caffeine and excess sugar.
6. Praise success; listen to parents' frustration; store drugs out of the child's reach; give medicine without drawing attention to the child.

## How the exam asks about it
Stimulant side effect/monitoring, or choosing structure and positive feedback.

## Related topics
[[Developmental Disorders]], [[Autism Spectrum Disorder]], [[Behavior Modification and Reinforcement]]

## Check against your textbook
- Pemoline has been withdrawn in many countries. Time to full effect in the handout (2 days) is unusual; verify. Current criteria allow onset before age 12.

title: Intellectual Disability
body:
## What it is
Below-average intellectual functioning (IQ below about 70) with significant limits in adaptive functioning. The handout uses the older term mental retardation.

## Must-know facts
- Causes: hereditary (Tay-Sachs disease, trisomy 21), pregnancy and birth problems (fetal malnutrition), medical conditions in infancy.
- Mild: IQ 55 to 69, "educable".
- Other levels, from common textbook teaching (handout cut off): moderate about 40 to 54 (trainable), severe about 25 to 39, profound below about 25 (needs total care).

## Priority nursing actions
1. Meet safety and basic needs first.
2. Teach in small steps with repetition; use concrete language.
3. Encourage self-care matched to level.
4. Support the family and arrange community services.

## How the exam asks about it
Match level to IQ range or to teaching capacity.

## Related topics
[[Developmental Disorders]], [[Autism Spectrum Disorder]]

## Check against your textbook
- The handout stops after the mild level; IQ ranges for the other levels come from general knowledge and should be checked.
